sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: California, United States Marine Corps. World War II, Korea and Viet Nam service. Date of enlistment, 1943-1976. Age of enlistment is 22 years old. Mr. McCain, when did you learn of World War II?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: What did I learn in World War II?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Learn of it.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I learned to keep my head down the best I could, although I didn't keep it down well enough on Iwo Jima. I got the top of my head shot off there. But I learned how to get along with people, about leadership and things like that, in World War II. And that's the big thing in the Marine Corps is leadership. I learned that while I was a young PFC on Iwo Jima there, but you still learn leadership and everything as it goes along.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Where were you when World War II started?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was at Texas A and M, back at College Station.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What were you doing when World War II started?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was going to college there at Texas A and M at that time. Then later on, I came out to California. My roommate and I -- the war wasn't very intensive at that time. My roommate and I, believe it or not, we hitchhiked out to California. Now, I had a ticket on a train because my father worked for the railroad and I had a ticket. But I didn't want to leave him. So what we used the ticket for was to check our luggage to Santa Monica, California, and then we got on and hitchhiked. And we didn't have any trouble, believe it or not, hitchhiking out to California. Got there and we went down and got our baggage. And we saved a lot of time that way. And then it's that time I got a job as a tool engineer for Douglas Aircraft. I had taken engineering back at Texas A and M and didn't have any trouble getting a job out there as a tool engineer for Douglas Aircraft at Santa Monica.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What were you building?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Airplanes, Douglas airplanes. We was really good. I was the one that -- We didn't design the parts. We designed the machines that make the parts. And we enjoyed that. That was good. And then the war got a little more intensive, and then I decided I wanted to become in the Marine Corps. And at that time I said okay, so I went down to join the Marine Corps. And lo and behold, I couldn't pass the physical. And the reason I couldn't pass the physical, in my younger days, I played football. And we had a play -- one play where we pull the guard and the tackle and I run and block the kick. And I got there too fast one day and the guy kicked me instead of the ball and broke three of my ribs and scarred my lungs. So they had an x-ray. And they found I had a scar on my lung and said, We can't use you. So I didn't know what to do. So I went back and was still working for Douglas Aircraft. And about that time they started taking draftees in the Marine Corps. They hadn't taken draftees before. And so I said now's my chance. So I went back to the recruiting station down there -- at the induction station rather. And I found a guy that's the biggest hard-charging, biggest guy I could find that was making a bunch of noise. But he looked like he was really physically fit. So I went up to him and I said, How would you like to be a 4F. He was complaining about going into the service. He said, How much it going to cost me. I said, It's not going to cost you a thing. So he said okay. So I gave him my papers and I took his papers. We went back. And he took my papers, and I became a 1A. He became a 4F. So I gave him my papers. And I don't know who he was. Never saw him again. So I came back. And then I took -- hold my hand up and I became a Marine. And then I got to thinking, hey, I'm going to have to take another physical later on some time in my career in this Marine Corps. So I went to see a specialist, a doctor friend of mine who had a son in the Marine Corps. And I said, This is my problem. I said, How am I going to pass physicals. He said no problem. He said every time they tell you to take a deep breath and hold it, he said, Don't take a deep breath, let it all out and turn a little bit sideways and they'll never catch you. So for 33 years I got away with being physically fit in the Marine Corps. It worked out great.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Where did you go to boot camp?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: San Diego.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: MCRD?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. And, you know, boot camp was a funny thing. Boot camp, they say how hard a thing it is and things like that. But boot camp was really easy for me. Boot camp was a piece of cake compared to what I'd been going through at Texas A and M. At Texas A&M, they're really rough on you there. But boot camp was a snap. I had no problem at all at boot camp.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Was there a culture shock to you for the military life?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. Because that's -- Texas A and M is a military school. So that's all I was familiar with. That's why it was very easy for me, going to boot camp. I had no problem whatsoever with that. And I really -- everybody was telling how rough it was. And I was looking at them and I couldn't figure what they was talking about because it was such a piece of cake. But each to his own there. But I had an easy time going through boot camp.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Were there any memorable stories of boot camp?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No, not in boot camp. It's a funny thing though. Later on, the drill instructor there, the guy that's supposed to be the hardest thing, later on he was the one that recommended me for a commission. And we went through -- in fact, we both went through officer candidate school together. His name's on that list there (indicating), Gus (Lennerhorf). And I had no problem. He's the one that -- not when I was in boot camp but later on after I got back from Iwo, he's the one that recommended me for a commission.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: When you were leaving boot camp, what were your thoughts about joining the war?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: When I was in what now?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: When you were leaving boot camp.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: When I was leaving boot camp, I was anxious to get out of boot camp and get in combat. I was ready to go. I was what you might say kind of gung-ho because that's why I came in the Marine Corps, to go to combat. And I was ready and I was anxious and just couldn't hardly wait to get out of there and get going.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Where did you leave from?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: What do you mean where did I leave from?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Where? Did you leave from San Diego?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: To go where?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: To the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. I left San Diego. And the first place we went to was the Island of Hawaii. And we stayed there and trained there for three to four months. And then we packed out and we went -- at that time we went to Iwo Jima.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you do in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: It was just training out there, field exercises, you know, and live firing and things of this nature. We had a -- it was the big island of Hawaii. Most people don't realize it. But Hawaii is not full of palm trees and things like that. They had a lot of like a desert up there. This was the big island of Hawaii. And we trained up there and had a lot of open space. And that's where we were doing all of our training for Iwo.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was your job when you were in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, I was just a young -- I was a fire team leader. They break up the Marines into squads and fire teams and things like that. And I was a fire team leader. There's three people in a fire team, and I was a leader of that particular team.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What is a fire team?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: A fire team consists of a fire team leader and a rifleman and a Browning automatic rifleman and an assistant Browning automatic rifleman. Those are the three people in that particular fire team. And they have three fire teams to a squad. And they have three squads to a platoon. And they have three platoons to a company. And we had a lot of fun out there.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did it prepare you for Iwo Jima?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, yeah, it did. It helped us a lot. We got to do a lot of live firings. That's what happened more. Now, an unsual thing, a Browning automatic rifle is no light piece of equipment. It's kind of hefty. And I worked out a deal. They made me the Browning automatic rifleman, and I didn't want to carry the rifle. I liked the rifle, but I didn't want to carry it. So I traded it off with a guy to become the rifle -- and I was just carrying it -- his assistant, carrying a carbine, a light carbine. So that's what I carried. And I got away with it for a long time.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: When you left Hawaii, what were your thoughts about getting into actual combat and meeting the enemy?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was kind of anxious to get into combat with the enemy right away. That's what I joined the Marine Corps for. And an unusual thing, we made the landing on Iwo, and we was aboard ship for quite a while. And then we got off the ship, we got on an LST, got on a -- changed ship to an LST. And there we had these AmTracs, amphibious tractors. We made the landing with amphibious tractors and got ashore there. And I remember we landed this place on Green Beach, Green Beach, right below Mount Suribachi. There was a big wide open space there. So I remember I stopped to pick up some -- I'd always wanted souvenirs -- so something there that I saw, and I reached down and I picked it up -- I shouldn't have done it because it normally would have been a mine, but it wasn't. So I picked this up and put it in my pocket. And about that time I looked up and the rest of the platoon had gone past us into a clearing. And they looked at me like he might say look, like somebody looking at a snake about to snatch. I couldn't figure out why they were looking at me like that for. So I started to cross this clearing. And when I did that, I found out why. Across this -- and nobody said anything said to me. But on the other side of this clearing, one end, there was a Japanese machine gun. And I went a little bit cross that. I was carrying my M1 rifle, and I was carrying the M1 rifle on my right side. This guy opened up on me with machine gun, really coming in close, close to my rear end. Like I say, I was carrying this machine -- this rifle on my right side. And an M1 rifle, like all rifles, has a metal butt plate on it. It come in so close to me that it hit my metal butt plate, ricocheted off the metal butt plate. And remember the guy that's carrying the Browning automatic rifle? They shot and killed him. They shot three times, three rounds right there (indicating). That's how close it was coming to me. But it didn't touch me.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did that experience change your perception of combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Didn't change it. I just realized that some people was going to get killed and things like this. After the war, I went back to see the parents of this guy that got killed and I explained what happened to him. And they were glad I come back and talked to him and things of this nature. But I carried the BAR the rest of the combat there, and that worked out real fine. But it didn't change my idea about this because I realized that people are going to get killed and wounded and everything. What worried me more than anything else was people getting hurt, things like that. Like I hated to see a guy step on a mine or something like that or get in a hand grenade and get blown up by fragments of a hand grenade impregnated in you. But it was an experience. I'll tell you it was an experience.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Are you saying that it's better to be --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Are you saying that it's better to have been killed than to be maimed?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I personally would have rather have been killed than have both my legs blown off or something like that. And yes, I feel that it would be better to be killed than be wounded something like that.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Can you describe the first day on Iwo Jima.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: The first day?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, the first day, we made the landing, I guess about 8:00 o'clock in the morning. And they explained about going cross this opening and getting shot at. We continued up this series of dikes up there. So we went up, and we were going across this thing. We got up to the top of it. There's a bomb crater up there. So the platoon passed this. And I told the guys, well, we better take some cover because it's going to be night, and quick as night comes, they're going to have a lot of banzai attacks and things like that. So my squad got in this big -- pretty good-sized bomb crater and we set up some machine guns and the Browning automatic rifle out there. And sure enough, as soon as dark came, here comes banzai attacks and things like that. We managed to get in our -- which was really a godsend -- we found a guy that was a flame thrower operator. We found two of them. And they had their flame throwers fully charged and everything. So I remember they had this big banzai attack coming across there. And I wait cross fire the best we could, all our weapons and things like that, but they're still coming. So I told the guy with the flame thrower, I said, Now wait until they get to here and I want you to crossfire your flames. We stopped them just like that. And then later on in the operation, not then but later on, I learned from this flame thing, flames, we got a flame tank of napalm, and we would spray the ground in front of us in the daytime and then when they started coming at night, we would light it off, just kind of stop those guys.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Banzai attacks?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: The Americans made that name up?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No, I don't think so. I think that was the Japanese, banzai.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Would they yell that?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Would the Japanese yell that?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. They would holler "Banzai, Banzai," and things like that, come charging up the hill. And we were -- I think it was something about dying. And we would try to help them out as much we could, let them die.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How long did you spend on Iwo Jima? Days? Weeks?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was there for about a week, I guess. And I got shot up. I talked about getting my head shot off.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did that happen?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, I should have been more careful. But I stuck my head up and got shot up. It went through my helmet and took the top of my head off. And some of my buddies said I got shot on purpose. And the reason they said that was because I don't like to ride on a ship. And I knew we was going to leave there and we was going to go back on a ship. But when I got shot there, they took me out and flew me out of there. So they said, You got shot on purpose so you wouldn't have to go back on ship, they just fly you out. Which, of course was not true, but that's what they still believe that.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: You were wounded and they flew you off the island?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Where did you go?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: To Guam initially, to the hospital there. And then from the hospital I went to Hawaii. And then from there, I was sufficiently recovered. I went back. And when the outfit came back from Iwo, I was sufficiently recovered, not then, but I joined them in Hawaii. I was back in Hawaii again.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How much ground did you cover on Iwo Jima?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, let me see. That's the second year. Oh, I guess about two miles.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Two miles?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: In a week?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. It was a lot of artillery and a lot of napalm and things like that from both sides. Not from their side, they didn't have the napalm. But we had a lot of fighting going on there. It was something that I looked forward to. And, I mean I don't want to go through it again. I mean I don't mind, but it wasn't something that I would really enjoy and things like that. But like I say, I hated to see some of my buddies get torn up and lost an arm or lost a leg or something like that, step on a mine or something like that. I didn't particularly relish that. But, you know, of all the people that I've been in combat with, I've never seen one of my buddies that would turn and go the other way. They was always going forward. I guess that's a Marine tradition. Anyway, all of them have been going forward at a great clip. I was really glad to see that. I didn't think that any Marine would run. And sure enough, I never saw one of them turn the other way. It's always the other way. I saw too many of them get killed by needlessly exposing themselves to go out and get their buddies and dragging them back and things like that. But never once did I see one go the other way. A bunch of gung-ho guys.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: That is true Marine tradition.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Now you're back in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Recovering?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: You join up with your unit again?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, at that point I was recommended to go to officer's candidate school. That when they sent me back to the States to go to Basic school, which is at Quantico, Virginia. I joined up out there. That's an unusual thing. We was the first Basic class. Seniority means a lot in the Marine Corps. And the first Basic class, we didn't get our commission until after we graduated. The second Basic class, they started before we graduated and they got commissioned before they started. They were -- all the second Basic class is senior to the first Basic class, which really riled a lot of us guys. But nothing we could do about it. I was just happy to be a Marine.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was officer's training like?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, it was -- like I said, I had a jump on everybody because I had been to Texas A and M, which was kind of like an officer's training thing there. And they try to teach you -- leadership is the biggest thing they try to teach you, all about leadership and they teach you about the uniform and things of this nature. And we had to go through all the weapons, all the weapons, and we fired the ranges and things of this nature and learned about hand grenades and all that kind of stuff. But primarily leadership was the biggest key word there, trying to learn about leadership.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How do you teach leadership?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, they just continually give you an example of things of this nature about leadership, examples of what good leaders was and things like that, both -- you see, all the good leaders are not officers. Lots and lots and lots of good leaders are enlisted. In fact, we would have never won these wars without the enlisted leadership. And so I learned like that. But there's nothing you can really do about leadership. It's mostly by example, like going back and talking about good leaders, like talking about Napoleon and things like that and go back in these things. I enjoyed learning about leadership. Nobody knows all -- and I repeat, nobody knows all there is to know about leadership. You learn something new every day.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Where did you go after officer's training school?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Officer's training school, the first thing I went to was Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. I went there. And I had been going with my wife for a long time before that. And, in fact, she was staying with my mother and father out at -- in Slaton, Texas. And after I got down to Gitmo, I got persmission to get me -- in those days, you had to get permission to get married. I got permission to get married. I came back to the States, had leave, came back to the States, got married, took my wife down to Gitmo. And of all places we've been stationed, she thinks that's the best place we've ever been. And the reason for it was that's the only place she ever had a maid.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was life like on Guantanamo Bay?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was life like?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Life was real good there at Gitmo. That was about the time the war was about over and they had the old traditions and things like that. They had a lot of cocktail parties. Even though I didn't drink, I made all the cocktail parties. They had a lot of athletic events going on there. And I was very (foreign). And I was a coach for the basketball team and the football team and things like that, besides playing on some of the softball and baseball teams. And we had a lot of fun there. But she really enjoyed it. And she was the big thing that helped me out in my career all along. Sparky had been -- her nickname is Sparky. So she helped me out a lot. And I would say without her, I would have never made it.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: You wouldn't have been a colonel?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. Without her, I would have never made it.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: So by this time World War II was over?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you do between the wars?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Between the wars, let's see. That was after Gitmo. Well, I went to a couple of schools. I went to the armor school. I was a tank officer. I went to armor school through the Army. It was an Army school at Fort Knox, Kentucky. I went to two schools there, became better situated with the tanks and things of that nature.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you think of tanks?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I like them. I think they was really great. I don't think we could have won the war without the tanks. I was really enthused about tanks. I really am.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was it about them?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, the fact is that we had two types of tanks. We had the gun tanks. And the Marines had a flame tank that shot napalm out. And that was really something. And we could bring up -- they didn't realize how they could tell the difference. And the way you could tell the difference, they had two guns coming out of it. One was a flame gun, the other was a regular gun. But we would bring those tanks up and crossfire them at night and really stop anything coming by. Or when we were coming up and we were trying to take a pillbox and we had a difficulty doing it, we'd bring up a flame tank and we'd shoot flame in the aperture of the pillbox. And sure enough, they would come out of there, if they could, quite rapidly. But most of my time between the war was getting ready for the next one. And the next one was Korea, of course.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What rank were you this time?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was a captain.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was your job?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: In Korea?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: At the beginning of Korea, what was your job?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was a company commander of Charlie Company tanks. I guess of all my tours of duty in the Marine Corps, that was my most enjoyable time was in Korea. And the reason for it was I was kind of like my own boss. I was a company commander of Charlie Company tanks. And you'd be surprised at the number of people in the Marine Corps that don't know too much about the employment of tanks. So they sent me out to join a battalion that was out kind of like in a forward point there. And so I made some good friends with the staff out there. And they let me operate pretty much on my own. So we would get ready to make -- they was getting ready to fight. And I said no, I don't believe you do it this way. I said, Let's use the tanks. So we reversed our operation and used the tanks, and they come out loud and clear. And we won that war, I think. Now, it comes time for me, I got shot up a couple of times, got some of my teeth shot out here (indicating). And then I was in a tank explosion and I got my face all burned. I didn't want you to think I was born this ugly. And then after that -- you see, if you get hit twice over there, after the second time, they're gonna send you home. So I got shot the second time. And a corpsman who was taking care of me was going to make a report of it and then I was going to go home. And I said, Wait a minute, now wait a minute, don't tell anybody about this because I'm not ready to go home yet. And I says, My wife has already been upset because she got that first one about I got the Purple Heart and all that kind of stuff. I says, Do not tell anybody. So they didn't tell anybody. So I didn't have to go home. So later on, I got hit for the third time in Korea. And they were going to send me home, that battalion I was with. And I says, Now, wait a minute, we've got this big operation and you don't have anybody to take my place out here then. So they said, Okay, we'll let you stay a little bit longer. So I got to stay about two to three more months out there. And finally, the battalion commander said, I'm going to send you home. I said, Now wait a minute, you got -- He said no. I said, Let me take one more operation. And he said okay. So I led one more operation. I got shot again. But what the hell, Marines don't care.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How many times -- you got shot four times in your career?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah, but not bad. I mean, didn't lose no arm or leg or anything like that. I mean, I was still operating. And that's a big, big thing. If they'd have put a report in each time, I would have been long gone, and I wasn't ready to come home yet. I was over there doing a thing. In Korea is where I got the Silver Star. And where I got that, we were making an advance. And one of the infantry platoons was having a little difficult time there, and I found out about it. So I left my tank and I went over this hill, I was going to see how I could help them. And I found out that they were really disorganized there. I don't know why. But I think the platoon leader had been killed and the platoon sergeant had been killed and they were having a really hard time. So I kind of took over that platoon and then I finally motioned my tank to come up. And we got that out of there. And as a result of that operation, they awarded me the Silver Star. Not that I deserved it or anything. But they gave me the Silver Star for that.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How long were you in Korea?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was about a little over a year.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you do when you were not fighting?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: When I was not fighting, I was getting my platoon squared away and getting in good shape, mainly getting the tanks ready to go again because they'd always find something to do with the tank. Because -- to get them in good shape, there was always something going wrong with the tank. So you'd spend your time inspecting the tanks and getting them prepared for the next operation.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did the tanks hold up well?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah, they held up well, as long as you'd take care of them. That's the big thing. As long as you'd perform the maintenance and things like that and grease them when you're supposed to and change the oil and all the things you're supposed to do, if you keep all that up, what we call keeping the maintenance up, they'll last you forever.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Were there problems getting supplies to you?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. I never run across anything like that. Everybody was pretty good. And I always managed to keep a little extra on hand. So when they needed something, I always had a little extra on hand. So some of the other companies used to come by and try to get some stuff off me, and I always tried to help them out. But they realized that I always tried to anticipate and get a little extra supplies on hand, which is a good thing. If I hadn't have done it, I'd have been in deep trouble several times.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: World War II was the first major deployment of tanks in combat after World War I where they were developed.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did your training for tanks based on World War II tactics change for Korea?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: It didn't change much.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. The only thing is that in World War -- you see, there's a big difference between Army and the Marine tanks. And the biggest difference is the number, because the Army's got so many more tanks than the Marine Corps has. So we'd take better care of ours, it seems like, more -- better maintenance and things like that because we couldn't afford to lose one of our tanks. If we'd lose one of the tanks, man, that's a catastrophe. So we tried to keep our tanks in good operating condition all the time, ready to go. And it worked out fine for us.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was the tactics for commanding tanks in combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: The tactics were different. In the Army they used massive --

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Like the (32:08).

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: But in the Marine Corps you used the short tanks and mostly the tanks to support the infantry.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did you do that?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, you'd get together. And if the infantry was going up someplace against like, for instance, a pillbox, the tank would take the lead and try to knock out the pill box before the infantry got there.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What about on open terrain?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Open terrain, we were all -- we were in pretty good shape in open terrain. The only trouble is we'd move a lot faster than the infantry, so we would have to be watching very carefully we didn't run off and leave them. But they -- like I said, we had so few number of tanks that we couldn't afford to loose any of our tanks. So we stayed pretty close to the infantry because they protected us from somebody running up and throwing up a mine underneath one of the tanks or something like that. And we really appreciated the infantry in doing all this. And they appreciated us because we complemented each other.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Something big to hide behind?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Something big to hide behind for the infantry; they would hide behind the tanks?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. We let the infantry ride on our tanks as they wish. You see, the problem is if you get in a big firefight, they're going to try to shoot the tanks and the infantry would have to bail out. But we worked real good together. That's the key to success is working closely with the infantry, and we worked it real close there.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How many tanks were there?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: In my platoon, I had about five tanks because we had -- wait a minute. We had more than that. I had about 15 tanks.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Fifteen. And you were assigned to an infantry?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was what?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: You were assigned to an infantry?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was assigned to tanks.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Right, but your tank group --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Was supporting, was supporting the infantry.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How many men were you supporting?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, say a platoon.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How many men is that?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, my guess is we were supporting about 200 people out there.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How many men were in each tank?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: They have the tank commander and they have the gunner and they have the loader and they have the driver. So it's generally about four or five. But it's generally three or four -- four or five on each tank. But we like to keep some people in there because sometimes we need them.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did you feel vulnerable in an attack?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No, I didn't. The only time you felt vulnerable is if you started going through a mine field. And, of course, if you found out it was a mine field, you stop right away and backed up in your same track. But other than that, if they started shooting at you like 75-millimeter guns or something like that, you could always retaliate because you had a 75-millimeter gun on your tank, and later you had 90 millimeters on there. And you could really take anything under fire that took you under fire. As long as you could see it, you could generally beat them. The thing is not seeing them because they could fire at you before you could see them. You see, that's the problem right there. But we worked out real fine. I liked working for tanks.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was the largest round a tank could take?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: The largest what?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Round.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: That they shoot?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: No, that you could be hit by and not be severely damaged.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, it depends on the round. You see, lots of different rounds is large rounds, but they're not too effective. But you'd get some of these armor-piercing rounds and a 75-millimeter would penetrate a tank. And if you'd get one with the armor piercing, they was kind of deadly if you got hit in the right place.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did your tank ever get hit?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Not with anything fatal like that, no.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did it sound like when bullets, small rounds hit your tank?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, it sounds like somebody with a hammer hitting the side of a tank out there. That's what it sounded like to me. Different people -- sounded like different things to different people. Different types of round makes a different thing, like armor-piercing would sound different than a regular round. And you had to be very careful you didn't get hit by an armor-piercing because an armor-piercing would go (making audible noise) right through.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Would it bounce around inside the tank or go through the other side?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. It would kind of ricochet -- in different sizes and thing different things. But if it made a penetration -- you see, what happened, it made penetration but made parts of the tank inside flake off, and so there's parts of the tank would be flying around inside.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Not a good thing.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Not a good thing.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No no, not a good thing. First time I got some of my teeth shot out right here, (indicating) these shot out.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did that happen?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, I had my mouth open, and there's a round come whipping by right there and take it out.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: That's close.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, well. And then I was in a tank explosion and, like I said, got my face burnt. Like I said before, I didn't want you to think I was born this ugly. And then --

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did you get hit by a round and then the tank exploded?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. I don't know what happened. To tell you the truth, I don't know what happened. I just -- because it wasn't my tank that exploded. It was another one. I run up to give them assistance and it just (making audible noise) went up. And then I was out helping some guys repair their tank and some (38:44) came in, some mortar fire came in. And the other three times I got hit, it was fragments from mortar. I got hit in the lower arm and I got hit in the hand and things like that.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Were you out in the field?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: On maneuvers?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. We was out fighting.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Fighting?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. So we just -- you got to be careful all the time. Like you never know when you're going to get hit. Like let me show you. Let me take my coat off. This wasn't Korea. This was Viet Nam. I wasn't in Viet Nam yet.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Not yet. When they finally sent you home --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: From Korea?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: From Korea.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did you feel about your duty that you had done in Korea?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: How did I feel about what I did in Korea? I felt pretty good because I thought I did a pretty good job over there. And if everybody had done the same thing that I had done, we'd have been -- the war would have been over a long time ago. That's the way I felt. Of course, maybe that wasn't true. But that's the way I felt. That was the question, how did I feel.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How long were you in Korea?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I think I was there just about nearly a year.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: About a year. What did you do when you got home?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: When I got home... Let me think. I went on recruiting duty. I went on recruiting duty in Raleigh, North Carolina.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What rank were you when you ended Korea?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: When I left Korea, I was a captain.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Same as you went to Korea, you were a captain?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was recruiting duty like after serving in two conflicts?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, I was -- my job was, of course, to get young men or women to join the Marine Corps. And I did a -- in my judgment, I did a good job. I did a -- we did what we call a quota, they assign you so much quota to get. We made our quota every month while I was on -- the three years I was on recruiting duty. I was on recruiting duty in Raleigh, North Carolina. We enjoyed it. And if there were enough people there, we'd come out and make talks to the schools and things like that. And I enjoyed talking about the Marine Corps. And I was trying to give the guys the best scoop I could about the Marines. I tried to pick the ones out that I felt would make it in the Marine Corps. And you'd be surprised the number of people that can't make it, and I knew that they wasn't going to make it. So I tried to push them aside. And those were the ones that really wanted to come in.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: When you were recruiting, did you talk about your wartime experience?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I talked about everything. They'd ask you questions about what it was like to be fighting and things like that.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you tell them?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I told them about the same thing I'm telling you now, about how it was to fight over there and who we were fighting against and et cetera. And the only people we had trouble with was just the officials in the schools like the principals and things like that. We had a hard time getting in some of the schools out there. So I said, well, it don't make no difference to me. I don't have to go to the schools. I could get recruits without going to the schools. And so we did -- we had -- The officer in charge was named Cain, C A I N, and McCain. So we got our quota every month. This was in North Carolina. And then later they assigned us part of South Carolina because they had a little difficulty in South Carolina. So we took over part of South Carolina, and we made some quota down there also. But it worked out real good.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did you find that service to be mundane compared to combat training and combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Say that again.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did you find being a recruiter mundane and boring?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. I felt that it was just another job in the Marine Corps. And they have so many different jobs and I felt that that is important -- since I'd been assigned that, that it's just as important that I do a good job at that. So that's the way Marines are. They try to do a good job at every job they're assigned. So I tried to do a good job at recruiting and I was pleased with my operation there in recruiting.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Viet Nam, unpopular conflict?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: It was an unpopular conflict. How did you feel about being in the service with all of the bad political atmosphere?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, I kind of made fun of it. I couldn't understand why people would talk like that or acted like that. The biggest thing was these draft dodgers. I says I'm glad that they're draft dodgers because that's the people we don't want. So as long as they found out they're draft dodgers, let them go. We don't want them in the Marine Corps. And that's the way I operated.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Not everyone belongs in combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Not everyone belongs in combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No. I just felt that not -- yeah, that not everybody belongs in combat. Well, I feel all the Marines belong in combat.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: But sometimes sooner or later, it's all Marines should go to combat. And I think all Marines feel that way. I really do.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: But not all people?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Not all people, no. A lot of people don't believe in -- a lot of people, I feel, they got that big yellow stripe right up and down their back. They don't want to come in the service. And we had a lot of people, draft dodgers and things like that. But that's -- maybe I'm wrong in that because I leave it up to that individual, what they feel like. That's just how I feel. I know we've had a lot of Marines that we really think a lot of because they're really out there putting it out, trying to -- freedom for our country and things of this nature. And I encourage them to do that.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: As the build-up in Viet Nam was happening, where were you?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Where was I in building up? In Viet Nam? Let me think. It was in --

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Early '60s.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was in Quantico at that time. I was an instructor at command staff college.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What were you doing?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I was an instructor.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: For?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: For the Marine Corps and teaching tank tactics and things of this nature and leadership and things of that nature. In fact, I'll show you a card trick I used to use on them. I had a -- I think I still got it. I was a very unusual instructor there. There was a friend of mine who was a good instructor but he was always doing something unusual. And I was determined that I was going to be a better instructor than my buddy and I was going to be something more unusual than he was. In fact, one of the times I ended up bringing a horse -- bringing a horse into the class because -- I don't know what I was trying to point out. But I brought this horse in and got my daughter -- my oldest daughter, she was with horses. I had her ride it in, ride down the main thing -- had to be careful where I walked because I didn't want to step through a board, you know, and fall through. I couldn't bring it up on the stage because the stage wasn't that strong. So I just brought her to the bottom of the stage there and everybody couldn't believe that I brought that horse in there. But a lot of little things like that. And I'd use -- I did a couple of magic tricks for them. And, in fact, this card trick I'm going to show you in a minute, I did for the class. And I had this projector that's projecting out, and I had projected these five cards up there on the screen up there and had somebody pick one out. And it worked out real good. And I'll show you the trick after while.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Teaching leadership, how is it different being taught leadership to teaching leadership?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: It's harder to teach than it is to receive. It takes -- you really have to know what you're doing to teach leadership because each person receives instruction differently and each person looks at leadership a little different than the other guy. So it's very difficult to teach leadership, good leadership. And that's what I was trying to do is teach leadership and make them understand what it's all about. And maybe I was successful, maybe I wasn't. I don't know. But I'd like to think I was successful in that leadership teaching.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How would you do that, teaching history of leaders past?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah, that and various given examples of things like what happened, like in a combat situation, like making sure that you got all the supplies you need instead of -- what happens if you don't have all the supplies, what are you going to do. And give you examples like this and things like that, how are you going to get -- what's your objective if you don't have good leaders and good leadership. And I kept pushing this thing about -- see, everything in the Marine Corps revolves around -- believe it or not -- around combat. So to have good combat situation, you've got to have good leadership there. And to have good leadership, you've got to have good Marines, I feel. And so that's one of the things that I was pushing very hard, to have good Marines, good leadership and push this very hard to get them to understand how this would happen. I don't know if I'm making sense or not. But I really enjoyed it. I might be able to show it over the TV.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Okay. When were you told you were going to combat in Viet Nam?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: When was I told? Hell, I don't know. I was -- just kept wanting to go and came home to go and came pointing out to go.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: And they sent you?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. Well, you see, that's the thing. The biggest thing is everybody realizes you're not going to get promoted unless you go to combat. So we kept putting in to go to combat, and everybody wanted to go to combat, so they wanted to get it on their record. I wanted to get it on my record, but I wanted to go to combat also. That's a different thing. A lot of people just wanted to get it on their record. I wanted to go to combat because of the combat. I also wanted to get it on my record and I wanted to get promoted. But the biggest thing was to actually get into the combat, is what I was more interested than anything else.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Why was that, do you think?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Why was that? Some people just wanted to get it on their record?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: But you wanted to actually get into combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: And why was that?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Why was that? I don't know. That's just an in-grown feeling of being a Marine, I think. A lot of Marines are like that. But some Marines are not. I don't feel you're 100 percent Marine unless you really want to go to combat and you do everything you can to get into combat. And I did. I did everything I could to get into combat, and it's worked out.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you think of Viet Nam when you arrived?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you. The biggest thing, I was very appalled by Viet Nam because they wouldn't let us fight it. You see, they wouldn't -- instead of saying here, this is your mission, go up and take that mound up there, they'd tell you how to do it and all that kind of stuff. And you couldn't fight Viet Nam like you wanted to fight, like you should have fought. So we had so many restrictions. Like what we should have done, we should have -- before it started, we should have accomplished about a half a million folks, Army, Air Force, Navy and everything in one place. And then when the war started, we should have gone about a 45-day bombing mission out there and obliterated Hanoi and all the towns like that. Then the war would have been over. But no, they wouldn't let us do that. They were trying to tell us how to do it and not to do it this way and that way. So we were really working at a disadvantage. We wasn't running -- The Marine Corps, the Army or the Air Force -- the military wasn't running the military fighting over there. It was being run by some politicians and things like that. That's why I say I was very much against what was happening over there. If they'd have let us -- if they let the military run it, it would have been over a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Compare the morale of the men between World War II, Korea and Viet Nam.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Okay. The morale was highest in World War II. I feel it was the highest there. And then the next was Korea. And then the last was Viet Nam. Now, Viet Nam had got to -- some people feel that only the people who had been to Nam was the losers. They've seen so many movies and things like that of the veterans of Viet Nam that are druggies and things like that, which is not true. They had some fine people over there. They just wouldn't let us fight the war like we should have fought it.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Like you were trained?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. We were trained. If they'd just said Take Hanoi, and let it go at that, okay. But they said Take Hanoi but don't kill anybody on the way up there. And Take Hanoi but don't kill all the (53:36). But they wouldn't do it that way. They would just -- I was very disappointed the way they were handling Viet Nam. It's just like I said, they should have turned it over to the military and just said go, win.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did you get to meet any of the people of Viet Nam while you were there?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: The people of what?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Viet Nam. The Vietnamese, did you meet them?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Not the enemy, no. You're talking about meeting the enemy or who?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: The South Vietnamese.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I met a few of them. But the biggest problem, most of them didn't speak any English. I had difficulty with that. But the ones that I did meet and that could speak English, I had a good rapport with them. In fact, I was always giving out candy bars and things like that, which made a big impression on some of those people up there. Because they just -- can you imagine people that don't have anything. And a lot of those people didn't have anything, and I felt real bad about that. We had what we called an Arc Light. Arc Light, when the planes fly over and they open up their bombway doors and they punch a button and all the bombs drop out at once. And I've seen whole jungles disappear because of Arc Lights flying over. So you have four or five planes flying over and have an Arc Light and drop all their bombs at one time, and you can just imagine what a bomb on a jungle looks like with all the bombs falling at once down there. And it makes kind of a big bang noise also. But boy, they would sure take care of the enemy down there. And like I say, if they'd have let us fight that thing, if they'd have flew an Arc Light over, say Hanoi to start with, two or three of them over there, Hanoi and a couple other places up there, and invaded it, after that, the war would have been over, we wouldn't have all these casualties, 50,000 casualties killed.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Were you near the carpet bombing?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Were you near where the carpet bombing was happening?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Where the bombing was going on?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Carpet bombing from the B-52s.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I've been there -- they generally alert us where it's going to be. So we were generally within a mile of it or so.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: You could hear it?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And like I say, normally if you get on top of a hill and sit (56:06) in the jungle out there, you'll see the jungle just flatten out. But they really did a job out there. Like I say, if they'd have let us fight that war, we'd have won it a lot sooner.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: (Nodding head.)

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What rank were you when Viet Nam started?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: When it started, I was a lieutenant colonel.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: When it ended, you were a colonel?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. I got promoted just before I took over the executive office of the Fourth Marine Regiment. And that's when I got this (indicating).

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Where did you get that?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: That's in the northern part of (56:02). That's when my arm was shortened about that much (gesturing). And like I say, I was just about ready to take over the executive office of the Fourth Marine Regiment, and bang, this happened. And I was laying there and blood was coming out. So there's guys running around not knowing what to do. So finally, I had to grab one of the corpsman and I says, hey, look, you better do something here. You better start putting something in me because I'm losing a lot of blood. So then they starting putting some blood plasma in me trying to stop this up here. But they was having a hard, difficult time. But it was right in the midst of a rocket attack. That's what caused this here. So I was trying to tell people what to do and things like that. But oh, well, war is war.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did tanks work well in Viet Nam?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No, they didn't work too well there because what the terrain was and such. Where the terrain was okay, it worked great. But lots of places like in the jungle and in a lot of mud and things like that, your tanks just couldn't operate. In those areas they didn't work very well at all. But in the rest of the areas there where you had were rolling hills and things like that, tanks were really a godsend. They really worked great. And even when we had the flame tanks there, they worked great there.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Style of combat of your enemy --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Of what?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Of the enemy.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah, what about it?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How was it different between World War II, Korea and Viet Nam?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, in World War II they were more sophisticated in doing more about fighting. And in Korea, they wasn't sophisticated as now, but they were still pretty good fighters.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What do you mean "sophisticated"?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, they didn't have the weapons that we had. In Viet Nam is really a deplorable situation because like I say, it's deplorable because we should have won it over. And they didn't have the weapons that we had. They didn't have the leadership that we had and things of that nature. But still, they were doing a good job of fighting because they were familiar with the terrain and things of this nature. If they would have just let us fight the war, we would have been over a long time ago and it would have been much different. They didn't let us fight the war, though, like the military should have fought it.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: It brings back thoughts of, say, the American Revolutionary War --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: The British went to an unfamiliar area and fought a war within these fledgling States who didn't have the weapons, the tactics, the history. And the British soldiers were not green. They were experienced combat veterans, and the Americans were green. Did any of that sort of thing come into mind as you had time to contemplate about what you were doing in wars in the past?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No, I don't recall anything like that.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Do you think about wars in the past when you're in combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Just the now?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, right there, the guy in front of me, the guy in front can shoot him and the guy can keep from shooting me, that's the biggest thing you're worried about right there. At least that's what my experience has been. I just keep worried about what's going to happen if we were going to make an attack on this hill over here (indicating) and what are we going to do after we take the hill, where are we going from there. That's all the things kept worrying by me. And we was just trying to keep doing a good job.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How was the intelligence?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Intelligence was pretty good in World War II. It was fair in Korea. And sometimes in Viet Nam, it didn't exist.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Really. When you're fighting a guerilla war --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: -- like Viet Nam, intelligence is kind of irrelevant.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: You'd sure like to know what's going on though. It makes a big difference. It makes a big, big difference. I just hope we never have another war. But who knows. I feel that sometimes sooner or later, they're going to have to fight China.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Let's hope not.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I hope not too.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Being a veteran of three conflicts and a person who wanted to go into combat --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: -- what can you tell somebody who's never been in combat, what you've learned?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, the biggest thing you learn is you've got to get prepared. That's the big thing. When I say prepared, be prepared physically and mentally and morally to go to combat.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How do you do that? Physically is easy, you train your body.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How do you do the last two?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, it's not easy, the morally. And you got to believe in God and things of this nature. Morally, like I say, you got to realize that you're going to have to kill somebody. And that comes to your mind is what was God saying when you're going to kill some people out there. So you try to kill just the right people. When I say "right people," you don't want to -- you try not to get any women and children. And you try not to do anything to anybody that's been wounded. You try to take care of most of the people that you can. You always tend to say what would -- you try to go into combat and there was some women and children out there, you'd say what would Jesus do if he was standing here.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Did you help your enemies, the enemy soldiers when they were wounded?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we'd help them. And -- I mean, it depends. Now, if there was a whole bunch of them, you can't help them all. But if there's one -- if you're going up in a place and you yourself wounded this guy, then you want to try help them. And there's several reasons for that. One, if you help this guy out, maybe it gets some information from him. Because there, we'd try to help him and maybe get an interpreter there that speaks the language and things like that and show that you're trying to help him. And generally you could get some pretty good information from this guy.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you learn about life from combat?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Just try to keep living it. Oh, I don't know. I don't know. It's hard to say. Learned about life from combat; the biggest thing is try to stay alive and try to help other people and pray to God that Jesus Christ will have a good thought and look down on you with a good thought.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did combat prepare you for your civilian life?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, my first job after I got out of the Marine Corps was a director of the Navy Marine Corps Relief Society. That's a private relief organization that helps sailors and Marines and things like that. And I was right down my alley because as a colonel, I had all my troops I was responsible for. And so if I found one of them that needed something, I would know where to send him. So this prepared me to be prepared to help my Marines all along, and it worked out real great. The Navy Marine Corps Relief Society is an organization that really helps a lot of people in a lot of different ways. It gets no money from the government. It's all private donations and things of this nature. But it really does a great job. And the thing that makes the Navy Marine Corps Relief Society go is the volunteers. The majority of the people up there are unpaid volunteers. And it's -- most of them is wives of servicemen themselves. And it has really worked great. So this prepared me, being in the Marine Corps, to prepare me for what my troops were going to be needing later on. And I felt I did a good job in that area.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How long did you serve in Viet Nam?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, about a year.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: From when to when?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. What did my card say? I don't know. Maybe it's not on my card. Just a minute. Let me see if I can find it.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Was it the beginning of Viet Nam to about a year or two, '67? Yes. So that was about at the very beginning of Viet Nam?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. I was there about a year after it started.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you do when you came home from Viet Nam?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Came home from Viet Nam, I went to the hospital for my arm, this thing here, you know. And I was in the hospital for a while and then got out of the hospital and I think I had become a special services officer of Camp Pendelton. And then after that, my last tour duty was to go to Marine barracks in Guam and take over as CO of the barracks there -- become the CO of the Marine barracks in Guam. And that was really a pretty good tour of duty. And like I say, every place I've been, Sparky has helped me. Without her, I couldn't have never have made it. And while I was over there in Guam, we had an experience that happened that she really helped me out with. And that's when the Vietnamese started sending all their refugees to the States. Remember that?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: And so I got a call one day, the admiral says, You be prepared tomorrow to receive 50,000 Vietnamese the next day. I said yes, sir. And so we started getting them in the next day. And I didn't know what to do. So Sparky said, I'll give you a hand. So it seemed like every kid that came off that ship, little kid, would have dysentery. So he gave me practically a blank check, get anything I wanted out of the post (1:08). So I sent people down there to get bottles, you know, nipples and things like that. So they come off the ship there and they'd have these bottles of about that much (indicating) in the bottom of it, crudded milk and things like that. So Sparky would take them and throw them away and they'd say oh, no, no, no. And she'd throw the bottle away and give them a new bottle. And we had diapers by the bale because we'd need them. But every kid had, like I say, dysentery. So we got new diapers and new bottles and things like that. Then I had an idea. I said we got to put these people to work doing things that's going to help their own. So we started out, we found out we had -- some of them had doctors and some of them were nurses. So we got all those people and put them in one area working, things like that. They worked out pretty good. We even went so far as to -- I got a barber shop -- I found a barber shop and got to cutting guys' hair. And the ladies were all coming to me and saying I want something too. So I got a beauty shop for the ladies. So we really had a going operation there. But Sparky was responsible for all of this. She kind of honcho'd all this and it worked out real great. Well, if we hadn't had the help from the admiral, now, he really said you're going to get anything you want from the PX, that's when we got the bottles and the nipples and the diapers and things of that nature. Boy. And I guess we had that -- I guess they had a big problem when the Vietnamese came here to Pendleton.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I don't know. I was worried they were going to bring me back and put me in charge of the one here.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: So the Vietnamese boat people, as they were called --

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Boat people.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: They came to the military bases along the California coast?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: No, no. What happened, they evacuated them from Viet Nam, some of the people, and they brought onto the ships. And they dumped out the first group there at Camp Pendleton. And before that, they brought down a group at Guam and they were just getting them out of Viet Nam is what they were trying to do. Why, I don't know. I don't know why they want to bring them out of Viet Nam. I said leave them there. That's my thought.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: They were probably all the southern Vietnamese who were opposed to Communist rule.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I'd say leave them all there. It's their problem, let them solve it. I don't want to get involved in what we did.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Saved a lot of people, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, well.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What did you do after that?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: What was your next tour?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, my next tour was like I say, I was a paid special services officer. And then the next tour was Marine barracks in Guam. And then the next one, they decided to kick me out of the Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Thirty-three years after you joined?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Yeah. You see, they have the regulation in the Marine Corps, if you've got -- key word is commission. If you've got 30 years commission service and you're not a general, you have to get out. Now, I had thirty-three, but the first three was enlisted. But I had thirty years commission serviced and I had to get out. If I'd have known that, I wouldn't have made colonel. I enjoyed the Marine Corps. If I had to do it all over again, I'd do the same thing.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Why wouldn't you have made colonel?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Why wouldn't you have made colonel?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: What year did I make colonel?

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: No. Why wouldn't you have made colonel? You said if you'd have known that, you wouldn't have made colonel.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I wouldn't have made colonel because I wouldn't have had to get out. You see, commission service, if you're 30 years commissioned service and you're not a general, you have to get out.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: So if I hadn't have -- I was just saying that if I hadn't had got a commission of -- and not a colonel, maybe I would have stayed in the Marine Corps longer.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: I enjoyed the Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Can you think of anything else?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, I don't know. I don't know if the biography thing helps you or not.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: We'll submit that. I thank you for your time.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, I enjoy when I talk about the Marine Corps. I really do.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: It sounds like it.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: If I had to do it all over again, I'd do the same thing. I keep asking Sparky my wife, I said What do you think -- what occupation would you rather me be in if I hadn't been a Marine. She said, I'd rather you be a Marine. But we had a lot of fun. Of course, it's what you make it. If you don't like it in the first place, you're not going to do well, you're not going to like it ever. I liked it from the word go. That's why I had such a hard time getting in. It would have broke my heart if I hadn't ever got in the Marine Corps. But I'll tell you what; I really felt well by getting that guy to take that physical for me. And then later on finding out what I could do to keep -- stay in the Marine Corps, you know. Oh, me. Yeah. I've been shot up several times in this thing. Like I said, I got my teeth shot out, my face burned off and the top of my head shot off and my arm shortened about four or five inches. But it's all been a great, great, great career. And I don't look back and say I wish I had never joined the Marine Corps. It's the other way around, I wish I would have got in sooner. Like I said before, boot camp was so easy after going to Texas A and M, people don't realize, don't believe that. But it's true. Texas A and M is a -- their first couple of years is really hard on you.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: How did you get the nickname Jinx?

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Well, in a football game, it seemed like every time the other team needed five or ten yards, they'd come up over on my side or something and they'd get five or ten yards. And it seemed like every time we needed five or ten yards, I'd carry the ball. So finally the guy says, He's a jinx for both sides. I said yeah. But I enjoyed it. I enjoy sports and I've been a coach of a lot of sports like coaching basketball, softball, football, and, like I said, softball. And I participated in all of those. But I enjoy the sports and activities and things of that nature. But most of all, I enjoyed being a Marine. It really would have broke my heart if I hadn't got in the Marine Corps that day. I was really thinking when I got thinking about to getting this guy to take my exam for me. I don't know who he was and I'd never recognize him if I see him again. But he did it. And he was glad to, at least he said he was, because he was complaining about he didn't want to be drafted and didn't want to go in. So I said how would you like to be a 4F and he said how much is it going to cost me. He was willing to pay me money. I said it's not going to cost you a thing, do as I tell you.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: Thank you for your time.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Okay. I hope I answered all your questions.

sp.speaker: Jeffery M. Beers
sp.p: You did a great job.

sp.speaker: Gene M. McCain
sp.p: Oh, you're very kind.
